qv0a05zf47i06yulvlmtq4dd.name: Lloyd Hotel
lines: [1800-1945] 1. **Lloyd Hotel** (Oostelijke Handelskade 34; 1921) (E: "Lloyd Hotel and the Lloyd complex", qv0a05zf47i06yulvlmtq4dd): built by the Koninklijke Hollandsche Lloyd as a hotel for emigrants bound for South America, many of them Eastern European Jews fleeing pogroms, deloused next door before check-in; from 1938 the state housed refugees from Nazi Germany here; a hotel again. Who: Eastern European emigrants in transit, German refugees. Era: 1921-1940. Status: changed (now hotel). Evidence: existing place text; [nl.wikipedia, Lloyd Hotel](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lloyd_Hotel); [nl.wikipedia, Koninklijke Hollandsche Lloyd](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koninklijke_Hollandsche_Lloyd) (authoritative source still to add: Stadsarchief or Rijksmonumentenregister). Caveats: Jewish slice may also claim it; agree who writes the paragraph. Existing text already tells the story well.

[jewish-arrivals] 4. **Lloyd Hotel, the emigrants' hotel** (Oostelijke Handelskade 34; 1921) (E: "Lloyd Hotel and the Lloyd complex", qv0a05zf47i06yulvlmtq4dd): built by the Koninklijke Hollandsche Lloyd for emigrants bound for South America, mostly Jews leaving Eastern Europe, who were deloused next door before they could check in. In the 1930s it took in refugees. Who: Eastern European Jewish transmigrants, 1930s refugees. Era: 1921 to 1935. Status: changed (hotel again). Evidence: [Rijksmonument 523289](https://monumentenregister.cultureelerfgoed.nl/monumenten/523289), [Wikipedia (nl) Lloyd Hotel](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lloyd_Hotel_(hotel)), [Wikipedia (nl) KHL](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koninklijke_Hollandsche_Lloyd). Caveats: the live summary already tells it. The emigrants passed through rather than settled, so frame it as transit.

j5ynez7kwp0ww2j5z9gw3wo7.name: Binnen Bantammerstraat, the first Chinatown
lines: [1800-1945] 2. **Binnen Bantammerstraat, the first Chinatown** (Binnen Bantammerstraat; from c. 1911) (E: "Binnen Bantammerstraat, Amsterdam's first Chinatown", j5ynez7kwp0ww2j5z9gw3wo7): Chinese stokers brought in by Dutch shipping lines (kept in reserve as strike-breakers in the 1911 seamen's strike) lodged here between contracts; boarding-house keepers acted as shipping masters; in 1928 Kong Hing opened here, the first Chinese restaurant to draw Dutch diners (Josephine Baker posed in its door in 1932); in the 1930s slump laid-off seamen sold peanut biscuits in the streets and about 1,000 were repatriated. Who: Chinese seamen (mostly Guangdong and Zhejiang). Era: 1911-1940. Status: changed (ordinary street, bilingual street sign since 2005). Evidence: [IISG, The Chinese of Amsterdam](https://iisg.nl/collections/chinezen-zeedijk/chinezen.php); existing place text; [UvA Public History on Chinese-Indonesian restaurants](https://publichistory.humanities.uva.nl/blog/babi-pangang-or-foe-yong-hai-chinese-indian-restaurants-in-the-netherlands). Caveats: Kong Hing's house number not found. The postwar slice owns the Zeedijk temple; the cluster "Around the Nieuwmarkt, migrant Amsterdam" (q1ogooimbt808nocosyfc1nu) overlaps, pick one.

hx7dwu71gosab9zsoiknjyt1.name: Pathé Tuschinski
lines: [1800-1945] 3. **Pathé Tuschinski** (Reguliersbreestraat 26-34; 1921) (E: "Pathé Tuschinski", hx7dwu71gosab9zsoiknjyt1): Abraham Tuschinski, a Polish Jew who left in 1904 for America and got no further than Rotterdam, built Amsterdam's most famous cinema palace; in the 1930s its La Gaîté stage was one of the jazz rooms where Surinamese, Caribbean and American musicians played night after night. Who: Polish Jewish emigrant; Black musicians. Era: 1904-1940. Status: open (cinema). Evidence: existing text; [Stadsarchief, Jazz-jaren. Mensen, migratie en muziek in Amsterdam 1930-1939](https://www.amsterdam.nl/stadsarchief/agenda/jazz-jaren-1/); [Wikipedia, Tuschinski Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuschinski_Theatre). Caveats: the La Gaîté jazz angle is new and could be an extra paragraph.

[jewish-arrivals] 12. **Pathé Tuschinski** (Reguliersbreestraat 26-34; 1921) (E: "Pathé Tuschinski", hx7dwu71gosab9zsoiknjyt1): Abraham Tuschinski, a young Polish Jew from Brzeziny, was on his way to America when he stayed in Rotterdam (1903 or 1904). There he started a kosher restaurant for transmigrants, then cinemas, and in 1921 he built this palace. Who: Eastern European Jewish (trans)migrant. Era: 1900 to 1942. Status: open (cinema). Evidence: [Rijksmonument 4828](https://monumentenregister.cultureelerfgoed.nl/monumenten/4828), [Jewish Currents: The uncivil servant](https://jewishcurrents.org/the-uncivil-servant-abraham-tuschinski-and-his-theater/), [IISG ondernemers: Tuschinski](https://www.iisg.nl/ondernemers/pdf/pers-1485-01.pdf). Caveats: sources give 1903 or 1904 for the stay in Rotterdam. The live summary already says "Polish Jewish emigrant".

mer1sei0s134fwgjvf9t02k8.name: Max Beckmann's exile studio
lines: [1800-1945] 4. **Max Beckmann's exile studio** (Rokin 85; 1937-1947) (E: "Max Beckmann's exile studio in a tobacco attic (Rokin 85)", mer1sei0s134fwgjvf9t02k8): the German painter fled the Reich the day after Hitler's "degenerate art" speech in 1937 and painted about a third of his life's work under this tobacco attic's glass roof, stuck here through the occupation. Who: German political/artistic exile. Era: 1937-1947. Status: changed (offices). Evidence: existing text; [Wikipedia, Max Beckmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Beckmann). Caveats: none; exile story is already the place's story.

az70tfshn2sculd3t521tiwc.name: Herberg Zeeburg, quarantine station and refugee camp
lines: [1800-1945] 5. **Herberg Zeeburg, quarantine station and refugee camp** (Zeeburgerdijk 633-641) (E: "Herberg Zeeburg, quarantine station and refugee camp", az70tfshn2sculd3t521tiwc): the city's quarantine grounds, whose empty barracks became a camp for Jewish refugees from Germany from December 1938 (Anne Frank's uncle Walter Holländer was held here a year). Who: German and Austrian refugees. Era: 1938-1940. Status: changed (the inn stands; barracks gone). Evidence: existing text; [Anne Frank House research site](https://research.annefrank.org/en/); [Wikipedia, Herberg Zeeburg (nl)](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeeburg_(Amsterdam)). Caveats: Jewish slice overlap.

[jewish-arrivals] 11. **Zeeburg quarantine station, the refugee camp** (Zeeburgerdijk 633-641; camp 1938 to 1940) (E: "Herberg Zeeburg, quarantine station and refugee camp", az70tfshn2sculd3t521tiwc): after Kristallnacht the empty quarantine sheds became a guarded camp for Jewish refugees from Germany, among them Edith Frank's brother Walter Holländer. A camp order dated January 1940 still survives. Who: German and Austrian Jewish refugees. Era: 1938 to 1940. Status: changed (the inn survives; the sheds are gone). Evidence: [Anne Frank House research: Jewish refugee camp Zeeburg](https://research.annefrank.org/en/locaties/63a9ac86-dcbe-449c-85de-be2e3561d374/), [Rijksmonument 6499](https://monumentenregister.cultureelerfgoed.nl/monumenten/6499). Caveats: the refugees were confined rather than welcomed, and the text should say so plainly.

y9cdoekn5uaiwedh0xanjzl6.name: The Colonial Institute's facade
lines: [1800-1945] 7. **The Colonial Institute's facade** (Mauritskade 62-64; 1915-1926) (E: "Read the facade of the Colonial Institute", y9cdoekn5uaiwedh0xanjzl6): the Koloniaal Instituut (now KIT and Wereldmuseum) was built for colonial trade and knowledge; its stone tells the colonial relationship that brought Indonesian and Surinamese students, servants and sailors to the city. Who: colonial connection (Indonesia, Suriname). Era: 1910-1945. Status: open (museum). Evidence: existing text; [Wereldmuseum Amsterdam history](https://amsterdam.wereldmuseum.nl/en); [Wikipedia, Tropenmuseum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropenmuseum). Caveats: it is the institution "that dealt with them", not a migrants' place; the extra paragraph should say so plainly.

rnfnkpvexon65qv8jlg3e9t1.name: Reestraat 6, where Anton de Kom lived
lines: [1800-1945] 8. **Reestraat 6, where Anton de Kom lived** (Reestraat 6; 1935) (E: "Reestraat 6, where Anton de Kom lived", rnfnkpvexon65qv8jlg3e9t1): the Surinamese writer, who came to the Netherlands in 1920, was deported back from Suriname in 1933, wrote Wij slaven van Suriname (1934) and died after resistance work in 1945, lived here in 1935. Who: Surinamese. Era: 1920-1945. Status: changed (only the ground floor of the old house survived). Evidence: existing text; [Canon van Nederland (window Anton de Kom)](https://www.canonvannederland.nl/); [Wikipedia, Anton de Kom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anton_de_Kom). Caveats: postwar slice may claim the Bijlmer monument (gpqpa6wg4twhxhjy8fsvaq77); this house is the pre-war one.

akzx2lcqjzqw8sxum6qcavfl.name: Museumplein, the 1883 colonial exhibition
lines: [1800-1945] 9. **Museumplein, the 1883 colonial exhibition** (Museumplein; 1883) (E: "Museumplein", akzx2lcqjzqw8sxum6qcavfl): at the International Colonial and Export Exhibition 28 people from Suriname were shown in a "West Indian" tent and Javanese villagers lived in a mock kampong for the summer, photographed by ethnic "type"; it is the first large group of colonial subjects many Amsterdammers ever saw. Who: Surinamese and Javanese (forced display). Era: 1883. Status: gone (the ground is the square). Evidence: [Rijksmuseum, group portrait of Surinamese exhibited 1883](https://www.rijksmuseum.nl/en/collection/object/Groepsportret-van-Surinamers-tentoongesteld-op-de-Koloniale-tentoonstelling-Amsterdam-1883--2579b63e2783ce0a51822b1ea0cb8f61); [Bovenkerk in De Gids, DBNL](https://dbnl.org/tekst/_gid001200101_01/_gid001200101_01_0013.php); [Wikipedia, International Colonial and Export Exhibition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Colonial_and_Export_Exhibition). Caveats: the existing text mentions the exhibition only in passing; needs a careful, unsensational paragraph.

ti17h50ut2dgk0eevx7vhflo.name: Koninklijk Theater Carré
lines: [1800-1945] 10. **Koninklijk Theater Carré** (Amstel 115-125; 1887) (E: "Koninklijk Theater Carré", ti17h50ut2dgk0eevx7vhflo): a German circus family (Oscar Carré, born in Halberstadt) came to the Netherlands in 1863, played winters in Amsterdam and built this stone circus. Who: German. Era: 1863-1911. Status: open (theatre). Evidence: existing text; [Wikipedia, Oscar Carré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Carr%C3%A9); [Androom, grave at Zorgvlied](https://androom.home.xs4all.nl/biography/p023807.htm). Caveats: birth year 1845/1846 differs by source.

wanthsf989hpp4s401xp9iq9.name: Krasnapolsky, the tailor's hotel
lines: [1800-1945] 11. **Krasnapolsky, the tailor's hotel** (Dam 9 / Warmoesstraat 169; 1866) (E: "Krasnapolsky's Winter Garden and the power station behind it", wanthsf989hpp4s401xp9iq9): Adolph Wilhelm Krasnapolsky, born 1834 in Peine near Hanover to a family from Kiev, came to Amsterdam at 22 as a tailor, worked at the Winkel van Sinkel and in 1865/66 took over the Nieuwe Poolsche Koffiehuis, a café much used by German speakers, which he grew into the grand hotel. Who: German/Polish-origin. Era: 1856-1912. Status: open (hotel). Evidence: [nl.wikipedia, A.W. Krasnapolsky](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolph_Wilhelm_Krasnapolsky); [Anantara Krasnapolsky history (nl)](https://www.anantara.com/nl/grand-hotel-krasnapolsky-amsterdam/history); existing text. Caveats: takeover year 1865 vs 1866; "Polish" origin is family lore via Kiev; existing title is about the Winter Garden, the immigrant angle needs a paragraph.

uuisrd9acyvij4c8q238znen.name: Peek & Cloppenburg, Nieuwendijk to the Dam
lines: [1800-1945] 12. **Peek & Cloppenburg, Nieuwendijk to the Dam** (Dam 20, Nieuwendijk 168-170; 1885-2027) (E: "Peek & Cloppenburg: from the Nieuwendijk to the Dam", uuisrd9acyvij4c8q238znen): two clothiers from the Cloppenburg area of Oldenburg started in Rotterdam in 1869, opened on the Nieuwendijk by 1885 and moved into their limestone palace on the Dam in 1917; one of the German textile dynasties (with C&A, V&D, Sinkel) that built Dutch retail. Who: German (Oldenburg/Westphalia). Era: 1869-1917. Status: open (leaving the Dam in early 2027). Evidence: existing text; [Wikipedia, Peek & Cloppenburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peek_%26_Cloppenburg); [DUIC, Peek & Cloppenburg Utrecht](https://www.duic.nl/cultuur/verdwenen-winkels-peek-cloppenburg-aan-de-oudegracht/). Caveats: some sources call the founders Dutch merchants; their origin around Cloppenburg is the majority view.

egatu1m4gzff5z1dhwthzfmv.name: IJssalon Koco
lines: [1800-1945] 13. **IJssalon Koco** (Van Woustraat 149; 1941) (E: "IJssalon Koco, where the road to the February Strike began", egatu1m4gzff5z1dhwthzfmv): ice-cream parlour of two German-Jewish refugees, Ernst Cahn and Alfred Kohn; the fight there on 19 February 1941 led to Cahn being the first person executed by firing squad in the occupied Netherlands. Who: German-Jewish refugees. Era: 1930s-1941. Status: changed (stone by the door). Evidence: existing text; [Wikipedia, Ernst Cahn](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Cahn); [Joods Monument](https://www.joodsmonument.nl/). Caveats: Jewish slice overlap.

[jewish-arrivals] 19. **IJssalon Koco** (Van Woustraat 149; 1941) (E: "IJssalon Koco, where the road to the February Strike began", egatu1m4gzff5z1dhwthzfmv): an ice-cream parlour run by two German Jewish refugees, Ernst Cahn and Alfred Kohn. Cahn became the first person executed by firing squad in the occupied Netherlands. Who: German Jewish refugees. Era: 1933 to 1941. Status: changed (shop; plaque). Evidence: [4en5mei (1471)](https://www.4en5mei.nl/oorlogsmonumenten/zoeken/1471/amsterdam-plaquette-op-de-gevel-van-de-voormalige-ijssalon-koco), [Wikipedia (nl) Ernst Cahn](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernst_Cahn), [NH Nieuws](https://www.nhnieuws.nl/nieuws/318293/ijssalon-koco-joodse-knokploeg-februaristaking/). Caveats: none.

qqrvdnqxlfk1cilbdfbyputg.name: International Institute of Social History
lines: [1800-1945] 14. **International Institute of Social History** (founded at Keizersgracht 264 in 1935; now Cruquiusweg 31) (E: "International Institute of Social History (IISG)", qqrvdnqxlfk1cilbdfbyputg): N.W. Posthumus set it up in 1935 to rescue the archives of movements persecuted in Germany, Austria and Russia, with exiles such as the Russian Menshevik Boris Nikolaevsky; in 1938 it acquired the exiled German SPD's archive with the Marx and Engels papers; it also holds the archive of the exile publisher Allert de Lange. Who: German, Austrian and Russian political exiles (and their papers). Era: 1935-1940. Status: open (at the later site). Evidence: [IISG, detailed history](https://iisg.amsterdam/en/about/history/detailed-history-iish); existing text; [IISG, Allert de Lange archive](https://iisg.nl/collections/allertdelange). Caveats: the live place is the Cruquiusweg building, not the 1935-1937 Keizersgracht house; the paragraph has to say where it began.

tppsxewme1azq9zi0zkuqa63.name: Jan van Eijckstraat 16, where the Wiener Library began
lines: [1800-1945] 15. **Jan van Eijckstraat 16, where the Wiener Library began** (E: "Jan van Eijckstraat 16: where the Wiener Library began", tppsxewme1azq9zi0zkuqa63): Alfred Wiener, a German-Jewish refugee, ran his documentation office against Nazism from here in the 1930s; the archive reached London in 1939. Who: German-Jewish refugee. Era: 1933-1939. Status: changed (flats). Evidence: existing text; [Wiener Holocaust Library](https://wienerholocaustlibrary.org/). Caveats: Jewish slice overlap.

[jewish-arrivals] 14. **Jan van Eijckstraat 16, where the Wiener Library began** (1933 to 1939) (E: "Jan van Eijckstraat 16: where the Wiener Library began", tppsxewme1azq9zi0zkuqa63): Alfred Wiener fled Berlin in 1933 and set up the Jewish Central Information Office here, collecting Nazi material. It moved to London in 1939; his wife and daughters, left here, were deported. Who: German Jewish refugee. Era: 1933 to 1943. Status: changed (house). Evidence: [Wikipedia (en) Wiener Holocaust Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener_Holocaust_Library), [Joods Monument: Expositur](https://www.joodsmonument.nl/en/page/700/expositur), [AD on the tribute](https://www.ad.nl/buitenland/eerbetoon-aan-afred-wiener-de-verzetsheld-die-de-gruweldaden-van-nazi-s-in-kaart-bracht~aad968b9b/). Caveats: none.

sg5x5jc3sih4rbjqsfsd6iny.name: Diamond Exchange, Belgian refugees of 1914
lines: [1800-1945] 18. **Diamond Exchange, Belgian refugees of 1914** (Weesperplein 4) (E: "Diamond Exchange on the Weesperplein (Diamantbeurs)", sg5x5jc3sih4rbjqsfsd6iny): when Antwerp fell in October 1914 about a million Belgians crossed into the Netherlands; with the diamond trade at a standstill, Belgian refugees were lodged in the exchange. Who: Belgian refugees. Era: 1914-1918. Status: changed (offices/hotel). Evidence: existing text; [Wikipedia, Belgian refugees in the Netherlands during WWI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgian_refugees_in_the_Netherlands_during_the_First_World_War); [1914-1918-online, Exile and migration (Netherlands)](https://encyclopedia.1914-1918-online.net/article/exile-and-migration-the-netherlands/). Caveats: the best Amsterdam site I found for 1914; "Alida Jacobsdorp" (refugee houses) could not be located.

owooq6lk1d1u4nf3ix7lguw6.name: Hirschgebouw
lines: [1800-1945] 19. **Hirschgebouw** (Leidseplein 23-31; 1882/1912) (E: "Hirschgebouw, the fashion palace opened for men only", owooq6lk1d1u4nf3ix7lguw6): Hirsch & Cie, a Brussels fashion house led by Leo Hirsch, a Jewish entrepreneur from Altena in Westphalia, opened on the Leidseplein in 1882; Nazi expropriation closed it in 1943. Who: German-Jewish/Belgian. Era: 1882-1943. Status: changed (Apple store). Evidence: [nl.wikipedia via Wikiwand, Hirsch & Cie](https://www.wikiwand.com/nl/Hirsch_%26_Cie); [Leiden, Depth of Field](https://depthoffield.universiteitleiden.nl/0501a02/); existing text. Caveats: an incoming firm rather than an immigrant family settling; middle strength.

rwae30mkxpyvv5tefp4hv8bv.name: Maison de Bonneterie
lines: [1800-1945] 20. **Maison de Bonneterie** (Kalverstraat 181-183 / Olieslagerssteeg; 1889) (E: "Olieslagerssteeg, the lepers' house, the oil pressers and Maison de Bonneterie", rwae30mkxpyvv5tefp4hv8bv): founded in 1889 by Rosa Cohen-Wittgenstein, born in Warburg (Westphalia) in 1867, and her husband, selling woollen socks; a department store by 1909. Who: German-Jewish. Era: 1889-1909. Status: open (store on Rokin/Kalverstraat). Evidence: [Amsterdam Museum, The founder of Maison de Bonneterie](https://amsterdammuseum.nl/en/topic/women-of-amsterdam/contribution/147745-the-founder-of-maison-bonneterie); [Wikipedia, Maison de Bonneterie](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maison_de_Bonneterie). Caveats: the original shop at 181 later housed H&M; existing place is a lane cluster.

lt6ywkmufnv86538dkwd63hx.name: C&A on the Nieuwendijk and the Damrak
lines: [1800-1945] 21. **C&A on the Nieuwendijk and the Damrak** (Nieuwendijk 193 in 1893; Damrak 70-79) (E: "Beurspassage, the 'Amsterdam Oersoep'", lt6ywkmufnv86538dkwd63hx): the Brenninkmeyer brothers were "Tödden", travelling linen traders from Mettingen in Westphalia; after Sneek they opened in Amsterdam in 1893 and from 1906 Bernard Joseph Brenninkmeyer built the cheap ready-to-wear formula here; their big Damrak store burned in 1963. Who: German (Westphalian). Era: 1893-1945. Status: changed (former C&A complex now shops, passage art). Evidence: [nl.wikipedia, C&A](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%26A); [Cofra Holding, heritage](https://www.cofraholding.com/en/about/heritage/beginnings/); existing text. Caveats: link to the Beurspassage is via the 1963 C&A fire only; might better be a new pin at Nieuwendijk 193 (current use unknown).

nu9fdr9m85u45ybyrzwehfke.name: Kaiser Wilhelm Schule
lines: [1800-1945] 24. **Kaiser Wilhelm Schule** (Vijzelgracht 9; 1908) (E: "Vijzelgracht corner, Walloon orphans, Holtkamp's cakes and a German school", nu9fdr9m85u45ybyrzwehfke): Jan Stuyt's school built for Amsterdam's German community; by 1934 De Tribune called it a Nazi school, and from 1942 the Dutch Nazi youth trained here. Who: German residents. Era: 1908-1945. Status: changed. Evidence: existing text (cites the 1934 Tribune); [Anne Frank House research on German schools in Amsterdam](https://research.annefrank.org/en/onderwerpen/7eaef6db-5d69-466c-a948-9d51fa897c9b). Caveats: only one independent source found; needs Stadsarchief confirmation. Shows the settled German community as well as the refugees.

cemiwv2z5qoml4p8tkr9rmz0.name: Gerhard Badrian's stone
lines: [1800-1945] 25. **Gerhard Badrian's stone** (Rubensstraat 26; 1944) (E: "Gerhard Badrian's stone, Rubensstraat 26", cemiwv2z5qoml4p8tkr9rmz0): a German-Jewish refugee turned resistance fighter, shot here in 1944. Who: German-Jewish refugee. Era: 1933-1944. Status: memorial stone. Evidence: existing text; [Joods Monument, Gerhard Badrian](https://www.joodsmonument.nl/). Caveats: Jewish slice overlap.

[jewish-arrivals] 29. **Gerhard Badrian's stone** (Rubensstraat 26; 1944) (E: "Gerhard Badrian's stone, Rubensstraat 26", cemiwv2z5qoml4p8tkr9rmz0): a German Jewish refugee who became a daring resistance man, freeing prisoners in SD uniform; shot here in 1944. Who: German Jewish refugee. Era: 1933 to 1944. Status: open (memorial stone). Evidence: [4en5mei (2509)](https://www.4en5mei.nl/oorlogsmonumenten/monumenten_zoeken/oorlogsmonument/2509), [Wikipedia (nl) Gerhard Badrian](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerhard_Badrian). Caveats: a refugee's story, but a resistance memorial. Optional.

c713iaaetg58mpsy5i5t1l4z.name: Truus Wijsmuller's bust
lines: [1800-1945] 26. **Truus Wijsmuller's bust** (Bachplein) (E: "Truus Wijsmuller's bust, Bachplein", c713iaaetg58mpsy5i5t1l4z): the Amsterdam woman who organised the Kindertransports of 1938-1940 that brought thousands of children out of Germany and Austria. Who: refugee children. Era: 1938-1940. Status: memorial. Evidence: existing text; [Wikipedia, Truus Wijsmuller-Meijer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Truus_Wijsmuller-Meijer). Caveats: Jewish slice overlap; she is the helper, not the arrival.

[jewish-arrivals] 17. **Truus Wijsmuller's bust** (Bachplein) (E: "Truus Wijsmuller's bust, Bachplein", c713iaaetg58mpsy5i5t1l4z): the Amsterdammer who met Eichmann in Vienna in December 1938 and got 600 children out, the start of the Dutch Kindertransports. Who: German and Austrian Jewish refugee children, and their rescuer. Era: 1938 to 1940. Status: open (monument). Evidence: [4en5mei Bachplein](https://www.4en5mei.nl/oorlogsmonumenten/monumenten_zoeken/oorlogsmonument/1438), [Stadscuratorium](https://stadscuratorium.nl/collectie/gedenkteken-truus-wijsmuller/), [Anne Frank House timeline](https://www.annefrank.org/en/timeline/63/jewish-children-taken-to-england-at-the-last-minute/). Caveats: this is a rescuer's monument, not a place the newcomers used. It pairs naturally with item 16.

refa3obwkah8361e9reb3uvt.name: Refugee house plaque, Zuideinde 443
lines: [1800-1945] 27. **Refugee house plaque, Zuideinde 443** (E: "Refugee house plaque, Zuideinde 443", refa3obwkah8361e9reb3uvt): 30 of the 75 Jewish refugees from Germany and Eastern Europe sheltered around Oostzaan in 1933-1939 lived in this one house. Who: German and Polish Jewish refugees. Era: 1933-1939. Status: plaque. Evidence: existing text; [Joods Monument](https://www.joodsmonument.nl/). Caveats: Jewish slice overlap; one of few Noord items.

[jewish-arrivals] 22. **Refugee house plaque, Zuideinde 443** (Oostzanerwerf, Noord; 1933 to 1939) (E: "Refugee house plaque, Zuideinde 443", refa3obwkah8361e9reb3uvt): 30 of the 75 Jewish refugees who came to this area between 1933 and 1939 lived in this one house. A rare memorial to arrival itself, in Noord. Who: German and Eastern European Jewish refugees. Era: 1933 to 1942. Status: open (plaque). Evidence: [4en5mei (2673)](https://www.4en5mei.nl/oorlogsmonumenten/monumenten_zoeken/oorlogsmonument/2673), [TracesOfWar](https://www.tracesofwar.nl/sights/24481/), [Joods Monument: Leo Mozes Rozenszajn](https://www.joodsmonument.nl/en/page/129325/leo-mozes-rozenszajn). Caveats: check whether the house is on the Amsterdam side of the Oostzaan border (the live record says Noord).

jnr5senvcx9anonwf0ijqybk.name: The Lloyd building on the Prins Hendrikkade
lines: [1800-1945] 28. **The Lloyd building on the Prins Hendrikkade** (Prins Hendrikkade 33; c. 1920) (E: "The Lloyd building, the 'gilded coffin' on the Prins Hendrikkade", jnr5senvcx9anonwf0ijqybk): the head office the Koninklijke Hollandsche Lloyd paid for from its wartime emigrant trade to South America. Who: emigrants (company side). Era: 1915-1922. Status: changed. Evidence: existing text; [Wikipedia, Koninklijke Hollandsche Lloyd](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koninklijke_Hollandsche_Lloyd). Caveats: weaker twin of no. 1; list only if the map wants the emigration business side.

[jewish-arrivals] 32. **The Lloyd building, Prins Hendrikkade 33** (1920) (E: "The Lloyd building, the \"gilded coffin\" on the Prins Hendrikkade", jnr5senvcx9anonwf0ijqybk): the head office the Koninklijke Hollandsche Lloyd built from the profits of carrying emigrants to South America, the same trade as item 4. Who: emigrants (largely Eastern European Jews). Era: 1914 to 1922. Status: changed (offices). Evidence: [Rijksmonument 518433](https://monumentenregister.cultureelerfgoed.nl/monumenten/518433), [Amsterdam op de kaart](https://amsterdamopdekaart.nl/1850-1940/Prins_Hendrikkade/33). Caveats: the emigrant trade of the First World War years was not only Jewish. A companion to item 4 rather than a strong item on its own.

nmmp3r0a58nbohv69ztzjvjq.name: Ons Suriname, founded 1919
lines: [1800-1945] 30. **Ons Suriname, founded 1919** (Zeeburgerdijk 19-23) (E: "Suriname Museum in the 1882 double school", nmmp3r0a58nbohv69ztzjvjq): the oldest Surinamese association in the Netherlands, founded in Amsterdam on 18 January 1919 as a Bond van Surinamers for the few hundred Surinamese then in the country; in this building since 1975, now the Suriname Museum. Who: Surinamese. Era: 1919 onward. Status: open (museum). Evidence: [DutchCulture, Society Our Suriname](https://dutchculture.nl/en/location/society-our-suriname); [NOS on the Suriname Museum](https://nos.nl/l/2527684); existing text. Caveats: building is postwar; coordinate with postwar-colonial slice, which will likely take it.

[postwar-colonial] 3. **Suriname Museum and Ons Suriname** (Zeeburgerdijk 19-23; association 1919, building since 1970s) (E: "Suriname Museum in the 1882 double school", nmmp3r0a58nbohv69ztzjvjq): home of the oldest Surinamese association in the Netherlands; here the Surinaams Historisch Museum opened in 1997 (closed 2005), The Black Archives grew from 2016, and Otto and Hermina Huiswoud have a prominent place at the entrance. Who: Surinamese. Era: 1919 to now. Status: open (museum; Black Archives back from Bijlmerplein 140 in 2026). Evidence: [Stadsarchief, 1997 Surinaams Historisch Museum](https://www.amsterdam.nl/stadsarchief/themasites/amsterdam-migratiestad/1997-surinaams-historisch-museum/); [DutchCulture, Society Our Suriname](https://dutchculture.nl/en/location/society-our-suriname); [Parool, Otto en Hermina Huiswoud](https://www.parool.nl/nieuws/otto-en-hermina-huiswoud-vroege-strijders-tegen-kolonialisme~b65a2eb0/); [The Black Archives returns to Oost](https://www.theblackarchives.nl/the-black-archives-keert-terug-naar-oost-in-april-2026.html). Caveats: sources differ on when the association moved in (1973 in a UvA chapter, 1975 in our text).

dhwxocbmhj09f1trc7yd828h.name: Waalse Kerk
lines: [early-modern] 1. **Waalse Kerk** (Walenpleintje 159 / Oudezijds Achterburgwal; refugees' church since 1586) (E: "Walloon Church and its gate of skulls", dhwxocbmhj09f1trc7yd828h): a friary chapel handed in 1586 to French-speaking Protestant refugees from the Southern Netherlands; galleries were added when Huguenots poured in after 1685, and the congregation still preaches in French. Who: Walloons, Huguenots. Era: 1586 to now. Status: open (services in French, concerts). Evidence: existing place text; [Wikipedia: Walloon Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walloon_Church,_Amsterdam) (lead); [De Gids 1985 on the Huguenot refuge, 50,000 to 60,000 to the Republic, Walloon poor relief took them in first](https://dbnl.org/tekst/_gid001198501_01/_gid001198501_01_0035.php). Caveats: existing text already tells the story well; maybe add a line that the Walloon deaconry was the first reception for Huguenots in 1685.

vn6ztawt9z1koc564tgmx9ub.name: English Reformed Church in the Begijnhof
lines: [early-modern] 2. **English Reformed Church in the Begijnhof** (Begijnhof 48; English since 1607) (E: "Begijnhof", vn6ztawt9z1koc564tgmx9ub; no separate place for the church): the beguines' church given in 1607 to English- and later Scottish-speaking Protestants; a 1927 tablet by Reformed Church in America clergy honours "the Pilgrim Fathers who settled first in the city of Amsterdam", and since March 2024 a bust by Fabio Pravisani remembers the Bergamo violinist Pietro Antonio Locatelli, who lived here from 1729 and is buried in the church. Who: English and Scottish Protestants, Italians. Era: 1607 to now. Status: open (Presbyterian services). Evidence: [ERC Amsterdam church guide (NL)](https://www.ercadam.nl/wp-content/uploads/2013/12/NLD.pdf); [HMDB: Pilgrim Fathers tablet](https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=291658); [HMDB: Locatelli monument, erected 2024](https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=311751). Caveats: the Begijnhof place mentions the English church in one line only; consider a separate place "English Church" for the list view rather than listing the whole Begijnhof. Pilgrim link: the Scrooby group passed through Amsterdam 1608 to 1609 before Leiden; do not claim they worshipped in this building (only a genealogy blog says so).

bd9zus4cc3pfaefl5qadav2s.name: Oude Lutherse Kerk
lines: [early-modern] 3. **Oude Lutherse Kerk** (Singel 411 / Spui; 1633) (E: "Oude Lutherse Kerk, the church behind the warehouse name", bd9zus4cc3pfaefl5qadav2s): the church of a congregation of German and Scandinavian migrants, who met in a warehouse from about 1600; services were in High German far into the 17th century, and sailors and labourers sat beside very rich merchants. Who: Germans, Danes, Norwegians, Swedes. Era: 1588/1633 to now. Status: changed (now UvA aula, still occasional services). Evidence: existing text; [Stadsarchief, 1734 Lutheranen helpen Salzburgse emigranten ("Migrantenkerk")](https://www.amsterdam.nl/stadsarchief/themasites/amsterdam-migratiestad/1734-lutheranen-helpen-salzburgse/); [Stadsarchief, 1663 Rel rond Deense dominee](https://www.amsterdam.nl/stadsarchief/themasites/amsterdam-migratiestad/1663-rel-rond-deense-dominee/). Caveats: add paragraph (the existing text says "many of them immigrants" only in passing). The 1734 story (Amsterdam Lutherans raising almost 23,000 guilders for Salzburg Protestant refugees stuck in Zeeland) is a strong extra hook.

y7r5f2euzhumkr6rzltq205s.name: Armenian church Surp Hoki
lines: [early-modern] 4. **Armenian church Surp Hoki** (Krom Boomssloot 22; 1714) (E: "Armenian church in a warehouse (Surp Hoki)", y7r5f2euzhumkr6rzltq205s): Armenian silk and jewel merchants, many from New Julfa in Isfahan and often called "Persians", made a warehouse their church in 1714; a new Armenian community bought it back in 1985. Who: Armenians. Era: 1714 to now. Status: open (Sunday liturgy). Evidence: existing text; [Stadsarchief, 1743 Armeniër trouwt met Amsterdamse](https://www.amsterdam.nl/stadsarchief/themasites/amsterdam-migratiestad/1743-armenier-trouwt-amsterdamse/); [Wikipedia: Voskan Yerevantsi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voskan_Yerevantsi) (first printed Armenian Bible, Amsterdam 1666 to 1668; lead only). Caveats: existing text is complete; could add the Isfahan origin. The Armenian press of the 1660s has no known address.

ps47axwum9uk96gvgg6xqliv.name: Walenweeshuis
lines: [early-modern] 5. **Walenweeshuis** (Vijzelgracht 2A / Prinsengracht; 1669 to 1671) (E: "Walenweeshuis, the Walloon orphanage waiting for a future", ps47axwum9uk96gvgg6xqliv): newcomers' orphans were not taken by the city orphanages, so the Walloon church built its own, first in the Laurierstraat (1631) and then this Dortsman block; from 1971 to 2016 it was the French consulate and Maison Descartes. Who: Walloons, Huguenots (later the French institute). Era: 1631 to 1967. Status: changed (empty, restoration announced 2025). Evidence: existing text; [NH Nieuws on its condition](https://www.nhnieuws.nl/nieuws/341809/zorgen-om-walenweeshuis-vijzelgracht-amsterdam); [Amsterdam Museum, "Doorgegeven Zorg", paintings of the Stichting Hospice Wallon](https://assets.amsterdammuseum.nl/downloads/Doorgegeven-Zorg_De-schilderijen-van-Stichting-Hospice-Wallon-1753805402.pdf). Caveats: overlaps with "Vijzelgracht corner, Walloon orphans..." (nu9fdr9m85u45ybyrzwehfke); list only this one.

jwu1v9y082kenwqqwx5tat5n.name: Ronde Lutherse Kerk
lines: [early-modern] 6. **Ronde Lutherse Kerk** (Singel 11; 1668 to 1671) (E: "Ronde Lutherse Kerk, the dome that was not allowed to be a tower", jwu1v9y082kenwqqwx5tat5n): built because the Spui church was too small "for the many Lutheran immigrants"; a dome because the migrants' church was not allowed a tower. Who: Germans, Scandinavians. Era: 1671 to 1935. Status: changed (hotel event hall). Evidence: existing text; [Stadsarchief, 1663 Danish minister: by 1650 Danes and Norwegians were nearly a quarter of the members](https://www.amsterdam.nl/stadsarchief/themasites/amsterdam-migratiestad/1663-rel-rond-deense-dominee/); [Wikipedia: Ronde Lutherse Kerk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronde_Lutherse_Kerk) (lead). Caveats: list this and no. 3 together or pick one if space is tight.

ozzqbokq676xfhwmw5yk7vni.name: Descartes's house
lines: [early-modern] 7. **Descartes's house** (Westermarkt 6; 1634) (E: "Westermarkt 6, where Descartes fathered a daughter", ozzqbokq676xfhwmw5yk7vni): the French philosopher lived in the Republic for some twenty years; the plaque of 1920 (Alliance Française) quotes his praise of Amsterdam's freedom, the classic refugee-thinker's testimony. Who: French. Era: 1634. Status: private house, plaque and pavement tile. Evidence: existing text; [HMDB: Descartes plaque, Alliance Française 1920](https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=131437); [Open Plaques: Descartes](https://openplaques.org/people/5402). Caveats: Descartes was a voluntary exile, not a persecuted refugee; say "came for the freedom" rather than "fled". Also "Westermarkt beyond the tower" (a1ludnk9q5hvxvgrj5rsnk1f) shares the address: avoid double listing.

ps4js53ffz8e85afl4tuahvc.name: Huis met de Hoofden
lines: [early-modern] 8. **Huis met de Hoofden** (Keizersgracht 123; 1622, De Geer from 1634) (E: "Huis met de Hoofden (House with the Heads)", ps4js53ffz8e85afl4tuahvc): bought in 1634 by Louis de Geer, son of a Walloon family from Liège, who recruited Walloon smiths to march to Amsterdam and ship out to his Swedish ironworks; his son Laurens housed the Czech refugee bishop Comenius here (marker: stayed 1656). Arrival and onward emigration in one house. Who: Walloons, Czech Brethren. Era: 1634 to 1670. Status: open (Embassy of the Free Mind museum). Evidence: existing text; [DBNL, Erflaters van onze beschaving on De Geer's Walloons walking to Amsterdam](https://www.dbnl.org/tekst/rome002erfl01_01/rome002erfl01_01_0013.php); [HMDB: Comenius marker, Keizersgracht 123](https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=227769); [Wikipedia: Walloon immigration to Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walloon_immigration_to_Sweden) (lead). Caveats: add paragraph on De Geer's Liège origin and the Swedish Walloons. The marker text is from HMDB, not checked on site.

rn7e0etakka9ta3b2ufe43fq.name: Nieuwe Waalse Kerk
lines: [early-modern] 9. **Nieuwe Waalse Kerk** (Keizersgracht 676; congregation's second church 1719, present building 1856) (E: "Nieuwe Waalse Kerk, now a museum of illusions", rn7e0etakka9ta3b2ufe43fq): the Walloon congregation, swollen by Huguenots, opened a second church in 1719 in an old bell foundry on the Prinsengracht; this replacement of 1856 kept the Huguenot congregation going into the 20th century. Who: Huguenots. Era: 1719 to 1959. Status: changed (Museum of Illusions since 2025). Evidence: existing text; [Wikipedia: Nieuwe Waalse Kerk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nieuwe_Waalse_Kerk) (lead); [Stadsarchief, 1862-1867 De hugenootse familie Boissevain](https://www.amsterdam.nl/stadsarchief/themasites/amsterdam-migratiestad/1862-1867-hugenootse-familie-boissevain/) (shows the Huguenot families' continuity; not read in full). Caveats: building is 19th century; the early-modern story is the 1719 church (gone, site on the Prinsengracht not pinned).

i9d2m7kfxk0r01n9ddltr8h7.name: Christ Church, the Anglican church
lines: [early-modern] 10. **Christ Church, the Anglican church** (Groenburgwal 42; congregation 1698, here since 1771) (E: "Christ Church, the English church in a cloth hall", i9d2m7kfxk0r01n9ddltr8h7): the English Episcopal congregation of 1698, for English merchants and soldiers who came after William III; windows show William and Mary and two English regiments. Who: English. Era: 1698 to now. Status: open. Evidence: existing text; [Stadsherstel: Groenburgwal 42 Christ Church](https://stadsherstel.nl/monumenten/groenburgwal-42-christchurch/). Caveats: overlaps the walk "Groenburgwal and Raamgracht" (e8fhx7glygq7g7jizf9c7mkz); list Christ Church.

wx8zwvbosc6wy8p6u7oygsh3.name: The Bruinistenkerk, church of the English Separatists (gone)
lines: [early-modern] 11. **The Bruinistenkerk, church of the English Separatists (gone)** (Barndesteeg, behind nos. 13-15, on the vanished Bruinistengang; built 1668) (E: "Barndesteeg, the penitents' convent and the mission hostel", wx8zwvbosc6wy8p6u7oygsh3, add paragraph; or N as its own gone place): English "Brownists" fled to Amsterdam from 1593; their church on the Lange Houtstraat (Vlooienburg, 1606) burned in 1662 and the remnant built this hidden church in 1668. By 1701 five members were left and joined the Begijnhof Presbyterians; the building became a notorious tenement, demolished 1910, and Tot Heil des Volks bought the site in 1915. Who: English Separatists (Pilgrim-era dissenters). Era: 1593 to 1701. Status: gone (Tot Heil des Volks hostel opposite). Evidence: [Ons Amsterdam, "Zelfs de politie waagde zich niet in de Bruinistenkerk" (Apr 2023), read via BrowserOS](https://onsamsterdam.nl/artikelen/zelfs-de-politie-waagde-zich-niet-in-de-bruinistenkerk); [Het Parool, 8 Apr 2023](https://www.parool.nl/amsterdam/van-godshuis-tot-rovershol-de-bruinistenkerk-was-verzamelplaats-van-zakkenrollers-en-ander-gespuis~bf8bda732/); [Wikipedia: Francis Johnson (Brownist)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Johnson_(Brownist)) (lead); literature: H. de la Fontaine Verwey, "Van kerk tot dievenhol", Amstelodamum 1949. Caveats: Ons Amsterdam names Ainsworth as founder in 1593, Wikipedia names Johnson; write "English Separatists led by Francis Johnson and Henry Ainsworth". Its 1593 meeting place "Engelse Pelgrimsteeg bij de Bakkerstraat" is unverified, leave out.

trm070oydav7jweh28oersju.name: Vondel's shop, child of Antwerp refugees
lines: [early-modern] 12. **Vondel's shop, child of Antwerp refugees** (Warmoesstraat 39, plaque; second plaque at Warmoesstraat 108; 1597 to 1650) (N for the plaque; E for his grave: "Nieuwe Kerk, the church without a tower", trm070oydav7jweh28oersju): the poet was born in Cologne in 1587 to Mennonite parents who had fled Antwerp in 1582; the family settled in the Warmoesstraat in 1597 and ran a silk and stocking shop; a plaque says he lived and traded at no. 39 from 1631 to 1650 and wrote the Gijsbrecht there. Who: Flemish (Antwerp) refugees. Era: 1597 to 1679. Status: plaques on later buildings; grave in the Nieuwe Kerk. Evidence: [HMDB: Vondel plaque, Warmoesstraat 39](https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=131301); [HMDB: "Hier woonde Vondel", Warmoesstraat 108](https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=218584); [DBNL, Biographisch woordenboek: parents fled Antwerp, Cologne birth](https://dbnl.org/tekst/bran038biog01_01/bran038biog01_01_4367.php); [Nieuwe Kerk handout on Vondel](https://www.nieuwekerk.nl/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/DNK-2024-12-19-Joost-van-den-Vondel-handout-spreads.pdf). Caveats: an 1879 study says the exact house cannot be identified; the two plaques disagree. Best as one N place "Vondel's Warmoesstraat" at no. 39 with the caveat, rather than list-adding the whole Nieuwe Kerk. Pool coordinates for no. 39 (HMDB): 52.37559, 4.89854.

aapv5y7n49dc05n4lzbswjbg.name: Noordse Bos weavers' houses
lines: [early-modern] 13. **Noordse Bos weavers' houses** (Spiegelgracht 27; Vijzelgracht 10 and 14-16; 1670) (E: "Noordse Bos, the weavers' houses of 1670", aapv5y7n49dc05n4lzbswjbg): the city gave free land for 400 houses that only cloth workers from outside the city could rent at first, many of them Walloons: an early state-sponsored scheme to attract skilled migrants. Who: Walloon and other immigrant weavers. Era: 1670 to 1672. Status: one corner house survives; others rebuilt 1870s. Evidence: existing text; [KNOB Bulletin (Bosman) on Amsterdam orphanages and the 1670s extension](https://bulletin.knob.nl/index.php/knob/article/download/Bosman141/250/295) (context, not read in full). Caveats: authoritative source for "many of them Walloons" still wanted (Abrahamse, De grote uitleg van Amsterdam, is the standard work). Medium strength.

q459if11mofdctbi93ajiglz.name: Our Lord in the Attic
lines: [early-modern] 14. **Our Lord in the Attic** (Oudezijds Voorburgwal 38-40; 1661 to 1663) (E: "Our Lord in the Attic (Ons' Lieve Heer op Solder)", q459if11mofdctbi93ajiglz): the attic church was built by Jan Hartman (1619 to 1668), a Catholic merchant born in Coesfeld, Westphalia, who made his fortune in Amsterdam. Who: Germans (Westphalian Catholics). Era: 1661 to 1888. Status: open (museum). Evidence: existing text; [Getty Conservation Institute, Our Lord in the Attic case study](https://www.getty.edu/conservation/publications_resources/teaching/case/olita/building/sael.html). Caveats: add paragraph on Hartman's origin; the existing text calls him a "stocking merchant", which I could not confirm.

y853cvdfiqbh4zi5qwky1nog.name: Rembrandthuis and the Black neighbours of the Jodenbreestraat
lines: [early-modern] 15. **Rembrandthuis and the Black neighbours of the Jodenbreestraat** (Jodenbreestraat 4; 1630 to 1660) (E: "Rembrandthuis (Rembrandt House Museum)", y853cvdfiqbh4zi5qwky1nog): archive research by Mark Ponte traced about a hundred Black men and women, many brought as servants or sailors through the Atlantic trade, living as free people around this street in Rembrandt's time; he probably used them as models. Who: free Black Amsterdammers (Africa, Brazil, Caribbean). Era: 1630 to 1660. Status: open (museum; 2020 exhibition "HERE: Black in Rembrandt's Time"). Evidence: [Rembrandthuis press release, HERE: Black in Rembrandt's Time](https://www.rembrandthuis.nl/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/press-release.-here-black-in-rembrandts-time.-the-rembrandt-house-museum-amsterdam.pdf); [DutchNews 2020](https://www.dutchnews.nl/2020/03/black-in-rembrandts-time-a-myth-shattering-exhibition-on-identity-and-truth/); [UvA (dare) record on the research](https://dare.uva.nl/id/d34f2ede-9e22-45eb-a216-382728b7916c). Caveats: add paragraph. Coordinate with `postwar-colonial` and `jewish-arrivals` (many worked in Portuguese-Jewish households): this is the place for the forced-migration side in this era.

[jewish-arrivals] 8. **Rembrandthuis and his Portuguese neighbours** (Jodenbreestraat 4; 1639 to 1658) (E: "Rembrandthuis (Rembrandt House Museum)", y853cvdfiqbh4zi5qwky1nog): well-off Sephardim bought houses in Rembrandt's block on the Breestraat and became his direct neighbours. He rented cellar space to them, painted Dr. Ephraim Bueno, quarrelled with Daniel Pinto next door, and the Talmud Tora synagogue stood behind his house. Who: Sephardic Jews. Era: 1600 to 1700. Status: open (museum). Evidence: [Mirjam Knotter, "Rembrandt's Jewish neighbors" (open access)](https://www.taylorfrancis.com/chapters/oa-edit/10.5117/9789463728188-4/rembrandt-jewish-neighbors-stroll-neighborhood-mirjam-knotter), [Rijksmonument 2029](https://monumentenregister.cultureelerfgoed.nl/monumenten/2029), [Jerusalem Post: Rembrandt and the Jews of Holland](https://m.jpost.com/jerusalem-report/rembrandt-and-the-jews-of-holland-578486). Caveats: avoid the 19th-century myth of Rembrandt as a friend of the Jews (curators dispute it). The claim that he sketched Menasseh ben Israel is weak. Stick to neighbours, leases and the Bueno portrait.

tbe0rj2l8it8w85ucvr0f9p5.name: Oost-Indisch Huis, where foreign crews signed on
lines: [early-modern] 16. **Oost-Indisch Huis, where foreign crews signed on** (Oude Hoogstraat 24; 1606 to 1798) (E: "Oost-Indisch Huis (East India House)", tbe0rj2l8it8w85ucvr0f9p5): crews were recruited here; for most of the VOC's life more than half its soldiers and close to half its common sailors came from abroad, above all from the German lands and Scandinavia, drawn to Amsterdam to sign on. Who: German, Scandinavian and other foreign sailors and soldiers. Era: 1606 to 1798. Status: changed (University of Amsterdam). Evidence: existing text; [UvA: Roelof van Gelder, Het Oost-Indisch avontuur. Duitsers in dienst van de VOC](https://dare.uva.nl/id/0465297a-7f69-4415-a686-737c65a5bcbe); [Big Think on Jelle van Lottum's figures](https://bigthink.com/strange-maps/dutch-golden-age-wasnt-all-that-dutch) (secondary). Caveats: add paragraph; percentages from a secondary summary, phrase as "more than half of the soldiers".

d8v11d37ehamcpmmyt32pxdr.name: Coymanshuis, an Antwerp family's house
lines: [early-modern] 17. **Coymanshuis, an Antwerp family's house** (Keizersgracht 177; 1625) (E: "Coymanshuis, Jacob van Campen's first known design", d8v11d37ehamcpmmyt32pxdr): Balthasar Coymans the elder (born Antwerp 1555) settled in Amsterdam in 1592 after a stay in Hamburg; his sons built this house, the very image of how the Antwerp merchant exodus made Amsterdam's fortune. Who: Flemish/Brabant merchants. Era: 1592 to 1759. Status: changed (offices). Evidence: existing text; [KNOB Bulletin article on the Coymans family and house](https://bulletin.knob.nl/index.php/knob/article/download/672/680/749); [Wikipedia: Coymanshuis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coymanshuis) (lead). Caveats: add paragraph; the existing text also carries the family's later slave-trade role, which fits the forced-migration thread.

z3csxegpxxglvahescux3ibv.name: The Lutheran orphanage
lines: [early-modern] 20. **The Lutheran orphanage** (Lauriergracht 116; 1678, front of 1784) (E: "The Lutheran orphanage on the Lauriergracht", z3csxegpxxglvahescux3ibv): the migrant church's own orphanage, needed because the city orphanage took only citizens' children; the swan of the Lutherans still sits in the pediment. Who: German and Scandinavian Lutherans. Era: 1678 to 1811. Status: changed (offices). Evidence: existing text; [Rijksmuseum: print of the new front, 1784](https://www.rijksmuseum.nl/en/collection/object/Nieuwe-voorgevel-van-het-Lutherse-Diaconie-Weeshuis-te-Amsterdam-1784--0346edf70487c72af50c637454b2d853); [Luthermuseum: Lutheran congregations and institutions of Amsterdam](https://luthermuseum.nl/en/tokens/lutheran-congregations-and-institutions-of-amsterdam). Caveats: add paragraph on why the Lutherans needed their own orphanage (the citizens-only rule: source it before writing; the Walloon text in the pool already states it for the Walloons).

qe1b2e08dtg739m19t7q4jfy.name: Van Brants Rus Hofje
lines: [early-modern] 21. **Van Brants Rus Hofje** (Nieuwe Keizersgracht 28-44; 1732 to 1733) (E: "Van Brants Rus Hofje", qe1b2e08dtg739m19t7q4jfy): founded for Lutheran women by Christoffel Brants, son of a cooper from Wittmund in East Frisia, who traded grain from Archangelsk, befriended Peter the Great and became Russia's man in Amsterdam. Who: East Frisian Germans, the Russia trade. Era: 1732. Status: changed (students' hofje). Evidence: existing text; [Luthermuseum, Lutheran institutions of Amsterdam](https://luthermuseum.nl/en/tokens/lutheran-congregations-and-institutions-of-amsterdam). Caveats: I could not confirm Brants's own birthplace (Amsterdam or East Frisia) in the archive index; keep to "son of a cooper from Wittmund" as the existing text has it.

wu8x1ee699pypv0gvq1a3rzq.name: Munttoren, the old Regulierspoort where poor migrants slept
lines: [early-modern] 22. **Munttoren, the old Regulierspoort where poor migrants slept** (Muntplein; 1597) (E: "Munttoren (the Mint Tower)", wu8x1ee699pypv0gvq1a3rzq): in October 1597 two brothers from Lyon, aged twelve and eight, were found begging and sleeping with many other poor newcomers in the arches of the town wall by the Regulierspoort, boarded up with planks and rags; they were given a pass to Zeeland. A plain picture of the hundreds of thousands who came hoping for work. Who: French, German, Danish, English labour migrants. Era: 1597. Status: the gate's tower stands. Evidence: [Stadsarchief, 1597 De broertjes Topin aan de bedelstaf](https://www.amsterdam.nl/stadsarchief/themasites/amsterdam-migratiestad/1597-broertjes-topin-bedelstaf/); existing text for the tower. Caveats: add paragraph; the arches were in the wall near the gate, not in the surviving tower itself.

c6jx4cj6mvvx6l95xrzgs15x.name: West-Indisch Huis and the Walloons of New Netherland
lines: [early-modern] 23. **West-Indisch Huis and the Walloons of New Netherland** (Herenmarkt 99 / Haarlemmerstraat 75; 1623 to 1647) (E: "West-Indisch Huis (West India House)", c6jx4cj6mvvx6l95xrzgs15x): the WIC's board met here; in 1624 its ship Nieu Nederlandt carried some thirty families, mostly Walloon refugees, to the Hudson, the first permanent settlers of what became New York: refugees who had arrived in the Republic moving on. Who: Walloons (emigrating), WIC colonists. Era: 1624. Status: changed (offices, John Adams Institute). Evidence: existing text; [Wikipedia: Jessé de Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jess%C3%A9_de_Forest) (lead); [Columbia Univ. Libraries: The De Forests and the Walloon founding of New Amsterdam](https://dlc.library.columbia.edu/durst/cul:prr4xgxd41). Caveats: add paragraph; numbers vary (30 to 34 families); de Forest himself did not sail. Also the house's link to the slave trade belongs to the forced-migration thread (coordinate).

istrimkx7o8g1yox4fm23k9f.name: Huis Bartolotti
lines: [early-modern] 24. **Huis Bartolotti** (Herengracht 170-172; around 1617 to 1620) (E: "Huis Bartolotti and the White House next door", istrimkx7o8g1yox4fm23k9f): the Bolognese merchant Giovanni Battista Bartolotti left his fortune to his wife's nephew Willem van den Heuvel on condition that he take the Italian name: an Italian immigrant's name written into the canal. Who: Italians. Era: early 17th century. Status: open (museum since 2026). Evidence: existing text; [Wikipedia: Huis Bartolotti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huis_Bartolotti) (lead, not opened). Caveats: weak as an arrival story unless an authoritative source on Bartolotti's own settlement is found; the Van den Heuvel family's Flemish origin unverified.

wgwo1e1v7iw7n4u00rgti7yi.name: Huis Marseille
lines: [early-modern] 25. **Huis Marseille** (Keizersgracht 401; around 1665) (E: "Huis Marseille, a map of Marseille on a canal house", wgwo1e1v7iw7n4u00rgti7yi): built for Isaac Focquier, a French merchant whose ship from Marseille made his fortune; his ties to the Walloon church suggest a French-speaking Protestant family. Who: French. Era: 1665 to 1676. Status: open (photography museum). Evidence: existing text; [Huis Marseille: the name](https://huismarseille.nl/en/history/the-name-huis-marseille/); [Caroline Hanken book fragment (2019) on the Fouquier family](https://download.boekhuis.nl/9789462085183_fragm-docb.pdf). Caveats: his birthplace is unknown; do not call him a Huguenot refugee.

fpmqosheztmndaoxhywua3g9.name: Lutherse Diaconiehofje (Konijnenhofje), gone
lines: [early-modern] 26. **Lutherse Diaconiehofje (Konijnenhofje), gone** (Konijnenstraat 16-48; around 1670 to 1909) (E: "Lutherse Diaconiehofje (Konijnenhofje) (gone)", fpmqosheztmndaoxhywua3g9): the Lutheran deaconry's almshouse for poor women of the migrant congregation; its gable stones went to the Lutherhof. Who: German and Scandinavian Lutherans. Era: 1670 to 1909. Status: gone. Evidence: existing text; [Luthermuseum, Lutheran institutions of Amsterdam](https://luthermuseum.nl/en/tokens/lutheran-congregations-and-institutions-of-amsterdam). Caveats: weaker; useful only if the list wants a Lutheran care cluster (orphanage, hofjes).

luch8lsv1dnvg5j9ivccgxfz.name: The Comenius stone
lines: [early-modern] 27. **The Comenius stone** (Valeriusplein; stone 1920, Comenius in Amsterdam 1656 to 1670) (E: "The Comenius stone: first stone of a monument that never came", luch8lsv1dnvg5j9ivccgxfz): the exiled bishop of the Czech Brethren spent his last fourteen years as a refugee in Amsterdam; the Czechoslovak state sent this stone in 1920 for a monument that never came. Who: Czech (Bohemian) religious refugees. Era: 1656 to 1670 (memorial 1920). Status: stone in the pavement. Evidence: existing text; [Radio Prague: Jan Amos Comenius, a Bohemian in Amsterdam](https://english.radio.cz/node/8088230); [Britannica: Comenius](https://www.britannica.com/biography/John-Amos-Comenius). Caveats: pick either this or no. 8 for Comenius, or both if the list allows; his grave is in Naarden (outside).

nbj11zik8thpzc180j9i4aa0.name: Compagnietheater, the Restored Lutherans' church
lines: [early-modern] 28. **Compagnietheater, the Restored Lutherans' church** (Kloveniersburgwal 50; 1792 to 1793) (E: "Compagnietheater (former Restored Lutheran Church)", nbj11zik8thpzc180j9i4aa0): the late-18th-century split of the migrant church; the breakaway built here. Who: Lutherans of German and Scandinavian descent. Era: 1793. Status: changed (offices, former theatre). Evidence: existing text; [Luthermuseum, Lutheran institutions of Amsterdam](https://luthermuseum.nl/en/tokens/lutheran-congregations-and-institutions-of-amsterdam). Caveats: by 1790 the congregation was largely Dutch-born; weak as an arrival story. Low.

qk6g2sa2qrnbncmq6wmbweu7.name: Schreierstoren and Henry Hudson
lines: [early-modern] 29. **Schreierstoren and Henry Hudson** (Prins Hendrikkade 94-95; 1609) (E: "Schreierstoren, the weepers' tower that probably wasn't", qk6g2sa2qrnbncmq6wmbweu7): the English captain hired by the VOC sailed from here in 1609; a 1927 plaque from New York recalls it. The place of departures, foreigners in Dutch service and the start of New Netherland. Who: English in Dutch service; emigrants. Era: 1609. Status: open (café). Evidence: existing text; [Wikipedia: Schreierstoren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schreierstoren) (lead). Caveats: more exploration than migration; low, include only if the list wants an emigration/departures marker.

u36dpf41xyomrrpcuh06gug5.name: Mozes en Aäronkerk
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 1. **Mozes en Aäronkerk** (Waterlooplein 207; hunger strike 7 to 15 Nov 1975) (E: "Mozes en Aäronkerk, the church named after two houses", u36dpf41xyomrrpcuh06gug5): about a hundred Moroccan workers facing deportation went on hunger strike in the church; it was the first time the legalisation of migrant workers became national news, and copycat strikes followed in Utrecht and The Hague. Today a cultural venue, Sant'Egidio services. Who: Moroccan guest workers (with KMAN, unions, churches). Era: 1975. Status: open (changed use). Evidence: Moslim Archief guide p. 50 (city PDF above); ONH "Wereldplek in Amsterdam: Mozes- en Aaronkerk verleende kerkasiel" https://onh.nl/verhaal/wereldplek-in-amsterdam-mozes-en-aaronkerk-verleende-kerkasiel ; Amsterdam750 "Wie waren de Kerkmarokkanen?" https://amsterdam750.nl/verhaal/kerkmarokkanen/ . Caveats: existing text already has a sentence on it; it deserves its own paragraph. Count of permits differs: "all 182" (Moslim Archief guide, existing text) vs "120 of the 182" (Zaans Museum https://zaansmuseum.nl/verhaal/de-lange-adem-van-de-182-kerk-marokkanen/ ); safest wording: "most of them".

[jewish-arrivals] 6. **Mozes en Aäronkerk, on the site of Spinoza's family home** (Waterlooplein 207) (E: "Mozes en Aäronkerk, the church named after two houses", u36dpf41xyomrrpcuh06gug5): Michael d'Espinosa, a Portuguese merchant, rented a house at the corner of the Houtgracht and Leprozengracht in the early 1650s. Baruch grew up there, round the corner from the synagogue that banned him in 1656. The church stands on the spot. It also links to the guest workers' slice: the 1975 Moroccan hunger strike was held inside. Who: Sephardic Jews. Era: 1600 to 1700. Status: changed (church, now an events venue). Evidence: [Spinozaweb: Houtgracht](https://spinozaweb.org/locations/5), [Rijksmonument 6305](https://monumentenregister.cultureelerfgoed.nl/monumenten/6305). Caveats: Spinozaweb says his actual birth house is unknown. Say "family home", not "birthplace".

vcugfm97az6grdhaubw4f1zs.name: Afrikahuis, Van Ostadestraat 268-270: the first Moroccan mosque and Casa Migrante
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 2. **Afrikahuis, Van Ostadestraat 268-270: the first Moroccan mosque and Casa Migrante** (Van Ostadestraat 268-270; mosque 1974 to 1982, African congregation 1994 to 2008, Casa Migrante now) (E: "Afrikahuis, Joop van Stigt's limestone church", vcugfm97az6grdhaubw4f1zs): in September 1974 Moroccan workers led by bookbinder Mohamed Echarrouti opened Amsterdam's first Moroccan mosque (later Al Kabir) in the basement the priest of this new Sint Willibrordus church offered them; later an African migrant church gave the building its name, and today the Spanish-speakers' drop-in house Casa Migrante (founded for Spanish guest workers) has its address at no. 268. Who: Moroccans, West Africans, Spanish and Latin Americans. Era: 1974 to now. Status: changed (temporary tenants; demolition threatened). Evidence: Stadsarchief canon window 41 (caption: "begon in de kelder van de ... Sint-Willibrorduskerk buiten de Veste in de Van Ostadestraat"); Amsterdam750 "Waar stond de eerste Marokkaanse moskee" https://amsterdam750.nl/verhaal/de-eerste-marokkaanse-moskee-van-amsterdam/ ; Moslim Archief guide (D4 "Van Ostadestraat 268 eerste locatie Al Kabir Moskee"); Casa Migrante history page https://casamigrante.com/nl/onze-geschiedenis/ (address Van Ostadestraat 268). Caveats: the strongest single building in this slice, three migrant layers in one. Casa Migrante founding year differs: 1961 (Casa Migrante, Kansfonds https://www.kansfonds.nl/artikelen/verhalen/de-mystiek-van-casa-migrante/ ) vs 1969 (Amsterdam750). Parool obituary of founder Theo Beusink (2019) says it long sat in the Spaarndammerbuurt: https://www.parool.nl/amsterdam/theo-beusink-1932-2019-beschermheer-van-spaanstalig-amsterdam~baf6291d/ . Check whether Casa Migrante is in this building or the neighbouring part before writing.

n55jul3695dglbhlg2rx9ky9.name: Gedenkteken Atatürk and the site of woonoord Atatürk
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 3. **Gedenkteken Atatürk and the site of woonoord Atatürk** (Atatürk, off the Klaprozenweg, Noord; hostel c. 1965/66 to 1978, monument 1978) (E: "Gedenkteken Atatürk", n55jul3695dglbhlg2rx9ky9): 34 white wooden barracks for 272 Turkish men, most of them NDSM shipyard workers recruited from 1967; residents founded Ataspor, struck over the food in 1972-73, and the hostel became the cradle of Turkish Amsterdam. Only the street name and the memorial remain. Who: Turkish guest workers. Era: 1965 to 1978. Status: gone (memorial and street name). Evidence: Stadsarchief Migratiestad "1972-1973 Bewoners Atatürk komen in opstand" https://www.amsterdam.nl/stadsarchief/themasites/amsterdam-migratiestad/1972-1973-bewoners-ataturk-komen-opstand/ ; Amsterdam750 "Wat was woonoord Atatürk?" https://amsterdam750.nl/verhaal/woonoord-ataturk/ ; canon window 41 (names "Atatürk Noord" and a second woonoord, Tussenhaven on the IJdijk). Caveats: existing text is already a full immigration story; list-add as is. Start year 1965 or 1966 depending on source.

jyvfr45sqhf2azxnzlcok9hx.name: De Duif, the second church of the "kerkmarokkanen"
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 5. **De Duif, the second church of the "kerkmarokkanen"** (Prinsengracht 756; summer 1978) (E: "De Duif, the first Catholic church back on the street", jyvfr45sqhf2azxnzlcok9hx): after Kamer debates and demonstrations, the Moroccan hunger strikers struck again here in summer 1978; on 17 October 1978 they got residence permits, and the regularisation was later widened to thousands more. Who: Moroccan workers. Era: 1978. Status: open (venue and church). Evidence: Moslim Archief guide p. 50; Amsterdam750 kerkmarokkanen; nl.wikipedia Mozes en Aäronkerk (citing Andere Tijden ep. 684 https://anderetijden.nl/aflevering/684/In-de-ban-van-koning-Hassan ); Leidsch Dagblad 17 July 1978 https://leiden.courant.nu/issue/LD/1978-07-17/edition/0/page/1 . Caveats: existing De Duif text has no hunger-strike mention; needs a paragraph.

w6ii28yzh82qznhc6q6z7zz3.name: Fatih mosque, Rozengracht
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 6. **Fatih mosque, Rozengracht** (Rozengracht 150; mosque since 1981) (E: "Fatih mosque, the new De Zaaier church the beauty committee lost to", w6ii28yzh82qznhc6q6z7zz3): the oldest Turkish place of worship in Amsterdam, bought by the Islamic Foundation Netherlands in 1981; the mihrab sits in the old main doorway. Who: Turkish guest workers. Era: 1977 to now. Status: open. Evidence: canon window 41 ("Het oudste Turkse gebedshuis, de Fatih-moskee"); Moslim Archief guide (B4/B5); NH Nieuws https://www.nhnieuws.nl/nieuws/338314/van-kerk-naar-moskee-de-succesvolle-metamorfose-van-de-zaaier-in-amsterdam . Caveats: existing text covers the conversion; add the first-Turkish-mosque framing and the Rokin start (item 7).

yvri4l2pqtmpvy3pwbvl5iuq.name: Nieuwezijds Kapel, where the Fatih mosque began
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 7. **Nieuwezijds Kapel, where the Fatih mosque began** (Rokin 78, now the Amsterdam Dungeon; mosque 1970s to 1980/81) (E: "Nieuwezijds Kapel, the Holy Place inside a shopping block", yvri4l2pqtmpvy3pwbvl5iuq): the hidden octagonal church behind the Rokin shops became the first home of the Turkish Fatih congregation before it moved to the Rozengracht. Who: Turkish workers. Era: 1970s. Status: changed (now Amsterdam Dungeon). Evidence: canon window 41 ("krijgt in 1977 onderdak in de Nieuwezijds Kapel en verhuist vier jaar later"); Moslim Archief guide ("in haar beginjaren ... Rokin 78, waar nu de Amsterdam Dungeon is"). Caveats: existing text says "a Turkish mosque followed (1972-1980)"; the canon says 1977 to 1981. Reconcile before writing.

xpau1hizqyb46l4qkkkrr7x7.name: Sint-Josephkerk, the Vluchtkerk
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 9. **Sint-Josephkerk, the Vluchtkerk** (Erik Roodenstraat / Robert Scottstraat, Bos en Lommer; squat Dec 2012 to 31 May 2013) (E: "Sint-Josephkerk", xpau1hizqyb46l4qkkkrr7x7): the empty concrete church where the rejected asylum seekers of We Are Here spent the winter of 2012-13, the first of many "Vlucht-" squats that gave the group its naming habit. Now a children's indoor playground. Who: refugees from Somalia, Eritrea, Sudan and elsewhere (We Are Here). Era: 2012-13. Status: changed. Evidence: Binnenlands Bestuur https://www.binnenlandsbestuur.nl/sociaal/ondermijning/asielzoekers-bivakkeren-in-gekraakte-kerk ; DutchNews https://www.dutchnews.nl/2012/12/greg_shapiro_sinterklaas_with-2 ; Stadsarchief Migratiestad "2013 Wij Zijn Hier" https://www.amsterdam.nl/stadsarchief/themasites/amsterdam-migratiestad/2013-wij-we-are-here/ . Caveats: existing text mentions the Vluchtkerk in one sentence; worth a paragraph.

uxgxywibm91l8g6i1jguv8yv.name: Corvershof and the Diaconie garden, where We Are Here began
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 10. **Corvershof and the Diaconie garden, where We Are Here began** (Nieuwe Herengracht 18-20; camp from 4 Sept 2012) (E: "Corvershof and the couples' homes behind H'ART", uxgxywibm91l8g6i1jguv8yv): a tent camp of rejected asylum seekers in the Protestant Diaconie's garden in September 2012 started We Are Here; the Diaconie's Wereldhuis for undocumented people works from the cellars here. Who: undocumented refugees. Era: 2012 to now. Status: open. Evidence: en.wikipedia We Are Here (citing Parool/Trouw) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/We_Are_Here_(collective) ; Stadsarchief Migratiestad 2013 page; Oxford COMPAS/CMISE paper https://cmise.site.ox.ac.uk/article/deserving-or-undeserving-governing-migrant-irregularity-and-squatting-in-amsterdam . Caveats: existing text says "later came students and refugees" but not this; Wereldhuis founding year not found (Diaconie pages only, mirror site).

yjoq70az9qtckl1pr91ogfro.name: Huis van Bewaring II, the Vluchthaven
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 11. **Huis van Bewaring II, the Vluchthaven** (Havenstraat 6; Vluchthaven Dec 2013 to mid-2014, asylum shelter 2015-16) (E: "Huis van Bewaring II, the prison that became the British School", yjoq70az9qtckl1pr91ogfro): the emptied remand prison where the city housed We Are Here members ("Vluchthaven"), then asylum seekers, before it became the British School of Amsterdam in 2021: refugees and expats in one building. Who: refugees; British and international expats. Era: 2013 to now. Status: changed (school). Evidence: en.wikipedia We Are Here (Parool 6 Dec 2013 "Havenstraat biedt iedereen hoop"; NRC 13 Dec 2013); existing text for 2015-16 and the British School; nltimes https://nltimes.nl/node/23836 (lead). Caveats: existing text lacks the 2013-14 Vluchthaven; confirm dates in Parool.

nrx2dgcndexsweb2agamfjtl.name: Bajeskwartier, the Bijlmerbajes as an asylum centre
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 12. **Bajeskwartier, the Bijlmerbajes as an asylum centre** (H.J.E. Wenckebachweg / Bijdorpstraat; AZC 2016 to 2018) (E: "Bajeskwartier and Bajesdorp", nrx2dgcndexsweb2agamfjtl): after the prison closed in 2016 its towers housed asylum seekers, many Syrians and Eritreans, until 2018; the "Wenckebachweg" of the brief is this site. Who: asylum seekers (2015 wave). Era: 2016-18. Status: gone (towers demolished, new district). Evidence: existing text; Vice https://www.vice.com/ro/article/refugiaiti-africani-duc-un-trai-deprimant-intr-o-fosta-inchisoare-olandeza (lead); COA/Parool needed. Caveats: one sentence now; needs a sourced paragraph (residents' origins not yet verified, do not state nationalities without a source).

n38rv2y627vrt24y1d101pae.name: Westermoskee (Ayasofya Camii)
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 13. **Westermoskee (Ayasofya Camii)** (Piri Reisplein 101; opened 1 April 2016) (E: "Westermoskee", n38rv2y627vrt24y1d101pae): the Turkish Milli Görüş congregation bought the site in 1993-94; 22 years of fights later Amsterdam's largest mosque opened, in Amsterdam School brick with a 42 m minaret. Who: Turkish community. Era: 1994 to now. Status: open. Evidence: Moslim Archief guide (essay by Emin Batman); NRC 2005 https://www.nrc.nl/nieuws/2005/05/07/het-bijzondere-van-de-baarsjes-10497086-a710231 ; Parool 2014 https://www.parool.nl/nieuws/na-jaren-gesteggel-is-westermoskee-bijna-af~b1a65d43/ . Caveats: existing text is good; add one line on who built it and why.

o5l8lm90go85kz7p8x50dmi8.name: Islamic burial ground at Westgaarde
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 15. **Islamic burial ground at Westgaarde** (Ookmeerweg 275, Osdorp; opened 1978) (N; the Tenerife monument in the same park is E, o5l8lm90go85kz7p8x50dmi8): Amsterdam's first Islamic graves, on the initiative of Turkish and Moroccan organisations in 1978, for those who could not or would not be repatriated; graves are never cleared. Who: Turkish, Moroccan, Surinamese Muslims. Era: 1978 to now. Status: open. Evidence: Moslim Archief guide p. 40-41 (with 1978 inauguration photo by Hans van den Boogaard, Stadsarchief); De Nieuwe Ooster/Westgaarde pages needed. Caveats: marks the moment migrants decided to stay; a sensitive place, keep text sober.

cz3wra0vbel3fdvf00rnyaug.name: De Kandelaar
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 16. **De Kandelaar** (Bijlmerdreef 1239; opened 2007) (E: "De Kandelaar", cz3wra0vbel3fdvf00rnyaug): a shared building for some fifteen migrant churches, designed with Ghanaian pastors, for congregations driven out of the demolished Bijlmer parking garages where they had met since the 1980s. Who: Ghanaian and other West African Christians. Era: 1980s to now. Status: open. Evidence: existing text; NH Nieuws https://www.nhnieuws.nl/nieuws/315601/in-amsterdam-zuidoost-zitten-meer-kerken-dan-cafes-maar-veel-daarvan-zitten-zonder-ruimte ; Streven 1996 on garage churches https://dbnl.org/tekst/_str010199601_01/_str010199601_01_0093.php . Caveats: good as is.

v7t4g2hg66ixsiqom0j8j1pf.name: Nossa Senhora de Fátima, church behind a doorway
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 17. **Nossa Senhora de Fátima, church behind a doorway** (Jacob Catskade 11; Portuguese-speaking parish since 1989) (E: "Church behind a doorway, Jacob Catskade 11", v7t4g2hg66ixsiqom0j8j1pf): a hidden 1919 church inside a housing block, home since 1989 to the Portuguese-speaking Catholics (Portuguese, Cape Verdean, Brazilian). Who: Portuguese and Lusophone migrants. Era: 1989 to now. Status: open. Evidence: existing text; Geheugen van West (cited in existing text); KDC Radboud database of Catholic migrant communities https://www.ru.nl/kdc/weten/katholieke-migrantengemeenschappen-nederland/ (lead). Caveats: the only Portuguese/Southern-European place I could confirm; composition of the parish not verified.

vwo6pkwzauz5odrly8amwtnl.name: Moeder Godskerk, the Syriac Orthodox church
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 18. **Moeder Godskerk, the Syriac Orthodox church** (Keizersgracht 220; Syriac since 1985) (E: "Moeder Godskerk (Church of Our Lady), Syriac and Catholic", vwo6pkwzauz5odrly8amwtnl): when the Redemptorists left, the Syriac Orthodox Church bought the canal church; it is shared with Catholic congregations, including a Surinamese one. Who: Syriac (Aramean) Christians, largely from south-east Turkey, who came as workers and refugees from the 1970s. Era: 1985 to now. Status: open. Evidence: existing text; en.wikipedia Church of Our Lady, Amsterdam https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Our_Lady,_Amsterdam . Caveats: the origin of the congregation needs an authoritative source before writing it.

svo2lgh22gzjlfc2qnj079g8.name: Dragers van verre (Nelson Carrilho)
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 19. **Dragers van verre (Nelson Carrilho)** (Westerpark; 1989) (E: "Dragers van verre (Nelson Carrilho)", svo2lgh22gzjlfc2qnj079g8): two bronze figures carrying loads on their heads, a monument residents asked for to the multicultural city, by a Curaçao-born sculptor. Who: all newcomers. Era: 1989. Status: open. Evidence: existing text; Kunstwacht/buitenkunstamsterdam (lead). Caveats: Amsterdam has no actual guest-worker monument (see Borderline); this is the nearest.

txtz9yb0h7h192isp9g7g7i2.name: Kapel en Convict, Ukrainian refugees' home and Circus Odesa
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 23. **Kapel en Convict, Ukrainian refugees' home and Circus Odesa** (Prinses Irenestraat 19; since 2025) (E: "Kapel en Convict: the high-rise monastery in the Beatrixpark", txtz9yb0h7h192isp9g7g7i2): about 150 young Ukrainian refugees live in the stacked monastery; the round chapel became a Ukrainian meeting place and café. Who: Ukrainians (2022 onward). Era: 2025 to now. Status: open. Evidence: existing text (sources there); Amsterdam750 "Van Kiev tot Weesp" for the wider Ukrainian story https://amsterdam750.nl/verhaal/van-kiev-tot-weesp/ . Caveats: very recent; good as the Ukrainian example.

nay21dj17ngqd8bux3eop03i.name: Former Buurthuis Transvaal, now BOOST
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 24. **Former Buurthuis Transvaal, now BOOST** (Danie Theronstraat 2-8; BOOST since 2017) (E: "Former Buurthuis Transvaal, Danie Theronstraat", nay21dj17ngqd8bux3eop03i): a listed 1970s community centre where refugees and other newcomers learn Dutch and find their feet. Who: refugees and newcomers. Era: 2017 to now. Status: open. Evidence: existing text; BOOST site (lead). Caveats: the immigration angle is current use only; short paragraph.

qmf435ep77ddd034uqcscc6r.name: WOW Amsterdam
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 25. **WOW Amsterdam** (Wiltzanghlaan 60; AZC from 2000 to the mid-2000s) (E: "WOW Amsterdam: technical school, asylum centre, art house", qmf435ep77ddd034uqcscc6r): a technical college turned asylum seekers' centre in 2000, now studios and a hostel. Who: asylum seekers (1990s-2000s). Era: 2000s. Status: changed. Evidence: existing text; COA/Parool needed. Caveats: little is known on the asylum years; medium.

va0zbmykdts05phe9rqvyr7k.name: Blauwe Moskee
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 26. **Blauwe Moskee** (Henri Dunantstraat 10; 2008) (E: "Blauwe Moskee, Henri Dunantstraat", va0zbmykdts05phe9rqvyr7k): mosque with Dutch-language services in Slotervaart, the first in Amsterdam to broadcast the Friday call (2019). Who: Moroccan-Dutch and other Muslims of Nieuw-West. Era: 2008 to now. Status: open. Evidence: existing text; en.wikipedia https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Mosque,_Amsterdam ; NOS https://nos.nl/artikel/2309517 . Caveats: existing text dwells on controversies; for this map frame it as second-generation, Dutch-speaking Islam, no politics.

uuu4k7ugqximblpgvc2vhx67.name: De Olijftak, El Hijra mosque
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 27. **De Olijftak, El Hijra mosque** (Arthur van Schendelstraat 17-18; mosque since about 1998) (E: "De Olijftak (El Hijra mosque)", uuu4k7ugqximblpgvc2vhx67): a Mennonite church that became a Moroccan mosque named after the Prophet's migration. Who: Moroccans. Era: 1998 to now. Status: open. Evidence: existing text; commons photo https://en.wikipedia.com/wiki/File:El_Hijra.JPG (lead). Caveats: part of a church-to-mosque cluster with items 6, 28, 29, 30.

ftaatjtntkp7bfct7wa170h9.name: Moskee Al-Ihsane
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 28. **Moskee Al-Ihsane** (Mendes da Costahof 32; 1993, new building 2017) (E: "Moskee Al-Ihsane", ftaatjtntkp7bfct7wa170h9): congregation that started in low business units and rebuilt in Dudok's style with a pattern from Fes. Who: Moroccans of Geuzenveld. Era: 1993 to now. Status: open. Evidence: existing text (Dudok society). Caveats: cluster item.

wb7nc43ioj44mvkl908j2ach.name: Moskee Nour, former Apostolic church
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 29. **Moskee Nour, former Apostolic church** (Witte de Withstraat 96; mosque since 1996-97) (E: "Former Apostolic church, Witte de Withstraat (now a mosque)", wb7nc43ioj44mvkl908j2ach): a 1921 Greek-cross church converted into a mosque and community centre. Who: Muslim community of De Baarsjes. Era: 1997 to now. Status: open. Evidence: existing text (register). Caveats: which community founded Nour not verified; cluster item.

hauwk3osq4hjs7dv3bfc5tz4.name: Broederhuis, Rembrandtpark
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 30. **Broederhuis, Rembrandtpark** (Orteliuskade 2-4 / Postjesweg 124; mosque 2003 to 2016) (E: "Broederhuis, Rembrandtpark (monastery, mosque, studios)", hauwk3osq4hjs7dv3bfc5tz4): a religious brothers' house that became a mosque, now studios partly for asylum-status holders. Who: Muslims of West; refugees. Era: 2003 to now. Status: changed. Evidence: existing text; Binnenlands Bestuur on the Aya Sofia occupation conflict with Stadgenoot https://www.binnenlandsbestuur.nl/bestuur-en-organisatie/verkiezingen/aya-sofiamoskee-voorlopig-niet-ontruimd (lead). Caveats: check whether this was the Milli Görüş "Aya Sofya" prayer house in the Stadgenoot dispute before saying so.

x72c3w4tdoi9rtzkylhdvkdf.name: Dappermarkt
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 32. **Dappermarkt** (Dapperstraat) (E: "Dappermarkt", x72c3w4tdoi9rtzkylhdvkdf): a 1910 market that became one of the most mixed in the city, with Turkish, Moroccan, Surinamese and Ghanaian traders. Who: all. Era: 1960s to now. Status: open. Evidence: Canon van Amsterdam window 48 (existing text); Moslim Archief guide on migrant market culture (Plein '40-'45 example). Caveats: existing text has no migrant angle and I found no sourced history of migrant stall-holders here; needs a source before a paragraph. Plein '40-'45 (Nieuw-West) is the guide's own example and may be stronger.

l1hdxidz2vtt8euo0agirndh.name: Bevrijde vogel, Sierplein
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 34. **Bevrijde vogel, Sierplein** (Sierplein; cube added 2024) (E: "Bevrijde vogel, Sierplein", l1hdxidz2vtt8euo0agirndh): war memorial whose new cube tells the war from Moluccan, Surinamese, Moroccan and Sinti angles. Who: newcomers' wartime histories. Era: 2024. Status: open. Evidence: existing text. Caveats: medium; overlaps postwar-colonial.

[postwar-colonial] 27. **Bevrijde vogel, Sierplein** (Sierplein; cube 2024) (E: "Bevrijde vogel, Sierplein", l1hdxidz2vtt8euo0agirndh): the war memorial's rotating cube now shows the war from Moluccan, Surinamese, Moroccan and Sinti angles. Who: several postcolonial communities. Era: 2024. Status: open. Evidence: existing text. Caveats: one source only (ours); add the stadsdeel announcement.

c55mx5b4m3jldspq9waen60w.name: A Happy Dog from Baghdad
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 37. **A Happy Dog from Baghdad** (E: "A Happy Dog from Baghdad", c55mx5b4m3jldspq9waen60w): mosaic by Iraqi artist Halim al-Karim on life as a refugee. Who: Iraqi refugees (1990s). Era: 1990s to now. Status: open. Evidence: existing text; Stadsarchief Migratiestad "1997 Tussen Amsterdam en Bagdad" (lead) https://www.amsterdam.nl/stadsarchief/themasites/amsterdam-migratiestad/1997-tussen-amsterdam-bagdad/ . Caveats: artwork only; medium-weak.

jo0k5dcfk52ngh4767k1u7a1.name: Groeiend Monument and De Boom die Alles Zag
lines: [guestworkers-and-new] 39. **Groeiend Monument and De Boom die Alles Zag** (Nellesteinpad, Bijlmer; 1992) (E: "Groeiend Monument and De Boom die Alles Zag", jo0k5dcfk52ngh4767k1u7a1): the Bijlmer air disaster struck flats full of newcomers, and many believe undocumented victims were never counted. Who: Surinamese, Ghanaian and other residents, documented and not. Era: 1992. Status: open. Evidence: existing text. Caveats: probably belongs to the postwar-colonial slice; listed here for the undocumented angle only.

[postwar-colonial] 23. **Groeiend Monument** (Nellesteinpad; 1992) (E: "Groeiend Monument and De Boom die Alles Zag", jo0k5dcfk52ngh4767k1u7a1): the El Al crash of 4 October 1992 hit flats full of newcomers, Surinamese, Antillean, Ghanaian and others, many without papers; the poplar that survived became the place of mourning. Who: Bijlmer newcomers of many origins. Era: 1992 to now. Status: open. Evidence: existing text; nl.wikipedia Bijlmerramp for victims and the amnesty for undocumented residents (verify). Caveats: victims' origins and the undocumented-residents follow-up must be sourced before writing.

mgbfdpu4kchmnsvxlbpoc56l.name: Portuguese Synagogue (Esnoga) and the Ets Haim library
lines: [jewish-arrivals] 1. **Portuguese Synagogue (Esnoga) and the Ets Haim library** (Mr. Visserplein 3; 1671 to 1675) (E: "Portuguese Synagogue (Esnoga)", mgbfdpu4kchmnsvxlbpoc56l): the descendants of Jews forced to convert in Portugal and Spain, who came to Amsterdam from about 1600 and returned to Judaism openly here, built the largest synagogue in the world in their day. Their library, Ets Haim, is still in the complex. Who: Sephardic (Portuguese) Jews. Era: 1600 to 1700. Status: open (synagogue and museum, part of the Jewish Cultural Quarter).
